comparisons.peer_topic: Potential Contractual and Contingent Cash Outflows
comparisons.peer_summary: Potential outflows considered in stress scenarios include debt maturities, deposit withdrawals, increased loan draws, and additional collateral calls, with credit rating downgrades potentially impacting these outflows and financial results materially.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and BAC explicitly incorporate credit rating downgrades as a key driver of increased cash outflows and collateral requirements in their liquidity stress scenarios. JPM assumes these outflows are non-contractual or contingent, while BAC details specific contractual outflows like debt maturities and loan draws that are exacerbated by downgrades. Both firms treat credit rating downgrades as a central factor impacting their ability to fund operations during stress.

sentences.text: Liquidity stress tests assume all of the Firm's contractual financial obligations are met and take into consideration:
• Estimated non-contractual and contingent cash outflows;
• Credit rating downgrades;

The types of potential contractual and contingent cash outflows we consider in our scenarios may include, but are not limited to, upcoming contractual maturities of unsecured debt and reductions in new debt issuances; diminished access to secured financing markets; potential deposit withdrawals; increased draws on loan commitments, liquidity facilities and letters of credit; additional collateral that counterparties could call if our credit ratings were downgraded; collateral and margin requirements arising from market value changes; and potential liquidity required to maintain businesses and finance customer activities.

Changes in certain market factors, including, but not limited to, credit rating downgrades, could negatively impact potential contractual and contingent outflows and the related financial instruments, and in some cases these impacts could be material to our financial results.

comparisons.peer_topic: Modeled Liquidity Outflow scenarios and modeling elements
comparisons.peer_summary: The Modeled Liquidity Outflow is based on multiple scenarios combining market-wide and firm-specific stress, including a 30-day horizon, a two-notch credit downgrade, and constraints on funding access without government support, covering both contractual and contingent outflows.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and GS model stress scenarios that include a specific credit rating downgrade (JPM lists 'Credit rating downgrades' generally; GS specifies a 'two-notch credit downgrade') and restricted access to funding markets. GS explicitly adds the assumption of 'No support from additional government funding facilities' and a 30-day horizon, whereas JPM’s disclosure focuses on the assumptions themselves (haircuts, downgrades, funding access) without specifying the exact horizon or government support assumption in the provided text.

comparisons.peer_summary: Stress scenarios assume no government support, limited access to equity and unsecured debt markets, repayment of maturing debt, higher haircuts for secured funding, and collateral requirements triggered by rating downgrades or disputes.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and MS assume that liquidity stress tests incorporate collateral haircuts and additional collateral requirements triggered by credit rating downgrades. MS provides more granular detail on funding restrictions (e.g., 'No access to equity', 'Repayment of all unsecured debt maturing'), while JPM broadly lists 'varying levels of access to unsecured and secured funding markets' and 'Collateral haircuts' as assumptions alongside rating downgrades.

sentences.text: Liquidity stress tests assume all of the Firm's contractual financial obligations are met and take into consideration:
• Varying levels of access to unsecured and secured funding markets;
• Credit rating downgrades;
• Collateral haircuts; and
• No access to equity and limited access to unsecured debt markets;
• Repayment of all unsecured debt maturing within the stress horizon;
• Higher haircuts for and significantly lower availability of secured funding;
• Additional collateral that would be required by trading counterparties, certain exchanges and clearing organizations related to credit rating downgrades;
